reverse_outline.summary: Chapter goal: learn business models, order economics and four scale stages, and how each shapes the architecture.
Three key points: a model assigns promises, each order metric stresses a platform part, and stages are shapes that make joins the problem.
The three failure patterns the chapter addresses: ill-fitting shared or split stacks, copying a giant's architecture, and an unmeasured peak.
The same jacket sold to a shopper and to a retail chain carries different conditions, which consumer software may not meet.
A marketplace sale adds the marketplace's rules, and operating a marketplace is another job; look-alike orders carry different obligations.
Locates the chapter in the book: the fictional brand sells the jacket through four business lines, each needing its own order route.
Roadmap of the chapter's sections, ending on the question of what four lines should share and keep separate.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: One Jacket, Four Ways to Sell It ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The company's 2026 revenue and margin split across four lines sharing one warehouse and catalog, reviewed before proposing a systems program.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: One Jacket, Four Ways to Sell It ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The engineering head asks each line's leader what they need from technology.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: One Jacket, Four Ways to Sell It ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: The online lead wants better checkout, delivery dates and marketplace stock; the wholesale lead wants correct contract prices, less retyping and no chargebacks.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: One Jacket, Four Ways to Sell It ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Operations wants warehouse work separated and store stock visible online; finance wants a single definition of an order.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: Setting the Scene at Kestrel & Pine: One Jacket, Four Ways to Sell It ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Each request reveals a distinct obligation, so the proposal must separate shared facts from line-specific rules.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Business Models, Defined by the People Who Report Them ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: The four lines are instances of business models, defined precisely by statistics agencies and annual reports, gathered in a table.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Business Models, Defined by the People Who Report Them ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Plain explanations of three reporting terms: seller of record, gross merchandise value and EDI-type sales.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Business Models, Defined by the People Who Report Them ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Business models coexist: the company runs four at once, and most multi-channel merchants run at least two.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What Each Model Changes in the Promise Chain ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: A business model decides who makes and keeps each order promise; a table assigns them for five models with architectural consequences.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What Each Model Changes in the Promise Chain ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Plain definitions of five table terms: punchout, parity rules, repricing, tenancy and a marketplace fulfillment program.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: What Each Model Changes in the Promise Chain ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Two rows matter most: who captures the order fixes where records originate, and who holds stock fixes how many locations availability covers.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Transition: public reports and statistics confirm at real scale the differences shown so far by definition and fiction.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Stores still carry most retail sales and even fulfil digital orders, so the architecture must treat them as a full channel.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: A brand's direct-versus-wholesale mix shifts yearly and can shrink, so the platform must serve both without rebuilding.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Operating a marketplace is a distinct business built around sellers, fees and payouts, so the book covers it elsewhere.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: In Practice: What the Public Record Says ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Business customers order both via web shops and via system-to-system messages, and wholesale architecture must handle both.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Unit Economics of an Order ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: What one order earns determines affordable promises; a table links each metric, its benchmark and the company's figure to a platform part.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Unit Economics of an Order ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Checkout abandonment reasons are really system failures to promise early || payment fees are an architectural and vendor-pricing choice worth six figures.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Same Jacket in Three Lines: A Worked Example ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Sets up a worked table taking one jacket's price and cost through three lines to per-unit contribution, with assumptions flagged.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Same Jacket in Three Lines: A Worked Example ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: The differing per-unit economics explain why each line wants different things from the platform, which must serve all three distinctly.
Orders cluster in time, and the peak is the load systems must be designed for, as public holiday-season figures show.
The company's own Black Friday peak: the storefront coped but stock sync and the warehouse queue failed, causing overselling.
Capacity belongs to the whole chain including integrations || the peak dictates when changes can launch, and wholesale has its own seasons.
Introduces four scale stages defined by business shape (channels, locations, countries, brands, who runs technology) rather than revenue.
The company's path through the first three stages, with its current problems located where several models share stock and catalog.
Vendor price tiers mirror the stages: fee drops and gated features show which decisions vendors expect at each size.
No public revenue threshold exists for buying hub systems; the signals are in the work, such as scattered data and multiple channels.
The author's triggers for considering product, order and warehouse systems, framed as reasons to investigate rather than thresholds.
Online growth has slowed, so mid-stage merchants compete on margin, returns and operations instead of traffic.
The company loses money where its lines share facts held in several systems and owned by nobody.
A silent price-sync failure made one storefront undercut other channels for days, caught by a marketplace; fix is one price owner plus reconciliation.
Running wholesale on a consumer platform leaves many orders hand-keyed and caused a retailer deduction over mismatched pallet labels.
Store stock never reached the web shop, so a collect-in-store pilot promised items already sold.
Two unconnected refund tools double-refunded returns; a high return rate demands a designed reverse flow.
Every failure surfaced when two copies of a fact were compared, often by outsiders, and was cured by assigning one owner.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Choices: One Stack, Many Stacks or a Shared Core ¶1
reverse_outline.summary: Fact ownership is a question of system arrangement; defines a stack and announces three ways to arrange stacks.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Choices: One Stack, Many Stacks or a Shared Core ¶2
reverse_outline.summary: Option one, a single stack for all lines: simplest and cheapest, until a line's promises do not fit the shop platform.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Choices: One Stack, Many Stacks or a Shared Core ¶3
reverse_outline.summary: Option two, a separate stack per line: best fit per line but duplicated records, the company's current troubled state.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Choices: One Stack, Many Stacks or a Shared Core ¶4
reverse_outline.summary: Option three, shared facts owned once with line-specific edges: the company's target shape, costlier and worthwhile only once joins hurt.

reverse_outline.draft_locator: The Choices: One Stack, Many Stacks or a Shared Core ¶5
reverse_outline.summary: Recommendation: keep one stack while it fits, switch to a shared core when a second system writes the same fact; avoid per-line stacks and copying operators.
Returns to the opening jacket: lines can share facts but not promises, and the scale stage says when single ownership pays off.
What is established: operational model definitions, message-based business ordering dominating, and measurable order economics with public benchmarks.
What depends on context: whether one stack suffices, whether the omnichannel stage is reached, and whether payment fees merit negotiation.
The author's own view: a model is who makes which promise, and the economics table maps where architecture must be strong.
Eight diagnostic questions for readers to apply the chapter's lessons to their own company.
Hand-off to the next chapter, which maps the parts of a commerce platform and what each owns.

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 50 outline summaries match the controlling idea of the spec paragraph their unit is aligned to, in spec order. The outline of p32a does not count 'four findings' and that of p36 does not say the message route is the larger; neither changes the idea.

The Unit Economics of an Order ¶2 (p18), marked two_ideas: its topic sentence ('Two observations follow for the newcomer') and the spec's controlling idea announce the two rows as one idea, numbers that look like design and finance matters and are architecture matters.

Seasonality and the Peak ¶3 (p22a), marked two_ideas: 'Two architectural facts come out of this' and the spec's controlling idea announce both facts as one idea. The closing sentence on wholesale seasons is spec evidence for the calendar fact; one flow reader found it tacked on.

Every unit traces to the supporting claim its section declares (S1 scene, S2 models, S3 promise chain, S2/S3 public record, S4 economics and peak, S3/S4 worked example, S5 stages, S6 incidents and choices). Two parts trace only loosely and are ruled on under flow_is_followable: the vendor's-roadmap sentence that closes p25 and the slowed-market paragraph p37, which serves as a bridge to S6 more than as support for S5.

Each of the six tables is introduced by a sentence saying what it gives, each of the six figures has a caption saying what it shows, and each statistic, quotation and scenario figure is followed by its reading (for example 'the store is still where most sales happen', 'The lesson for an architect is', 'In plain words'). Whether two of those readings follow from the figures is ruled on under flow_is_followable.

All other declared transitions (sections, paragraphs, conclusion and hand-off) are expressed at their boundary and pick up what carries_over names. In the two grouped sections the bold lead-ins carry the parallel relationships. The spec's own wording is inconsistent in two places without effect on the draft: p33 carries over 'five findings' where p32a says four, and p14 introduces 'four words' where its idea names five terms.

The introduction opens on a concrete case (one jacket sold to a shopper and to a retail chain), generalises it, places it in the running example and gives a roadmap; none of the weak patterns applies.

The conclusion opens by returning to the opening case and answering it, then sorts what holds by how settled it is. The 'Established' list restates figures from the body as compressed take-aways in the book's three-tier format, not as new body evidence, and no new subtopic is opened.

The first paragraph gives the synthesis (the lines share facts, not promises, and the stage says when owning the facts once pays). The so-what is in the author's synthesis (fill in the promise table, read the economics table as a map of where the architecture must be strong) and in question 8 on copied architectures; the refusal of a copied architecture is carried by that question and not stated in the prose.

The conclusion returns to the jacket sold to a shopper and to a retail chain and says what the software lacked: the two sales share the product record, price list, stock and order record, and each promise 'has to be kept at its own edge'.

The cold reader predicted the thesis and nine sections in the chapter's order; they map onto the ten sections, with the worked example folded into the unit economics, as the roadmap's own grouping has it.

The reader answered 'stage 2, Growing', 'heading towards' the Omnichannel transition, and argued only from channels, stores, models and shared stock, never from revenue. That meets the criterion's statement and the second alternative of the expected answer, though it leans further to Growing than 'Omnichannel': the stage table gives Growing 'two or three channels, first store' and the reader ruled Omnichannel out for want of wholesale and shared stock. The spec's open question on this probe stands.

All five answers match the expected ones: the marketplace captures the order and the brand imports it; the brand sets the price under parity rules; the brand is seller of record, holds the stock and ships.

The reader tied the 24% return rate to the reverse flow (restock, refund, credit note across systems), to be designed and not bolted on, and the 41-times peak hour to the capacity of the whole chain, every integration included, not only the storefront.

The reader gave the shared core with line-specific edges, triggered by the second system writing prices; shared are the product, price list, stock and order record, kept at the edges are the promises that differ (consumer checkout, B2B portal); a stack per line is not to be chosen.
